title: Scientists Threw These Animals Into Open Space. They Survived

scenes.text: Scientists shot tiny animals into open space. They came back alive.
They're tardigrades, or water bears. Under a millimetre long, eight stubby legs, and they live in moss and puddles.
In two thousand seven, a European satellite carried them 270 kilometres up and opened the lid. Ten days in the vacuum of space.
No air. Freezing cold. Cosmic radiation. Most survived. A few even survived raw sunlight, a thousand times stronger than on Earth.
Back home, they woke up, ate, and laid eggs that hatched normally.
Their trick is to dry out and shut down into a tiny barrel, protecting their cells until water returns. No animal had ever survived open space before. What else could they survive?

description:
Scientists shot tiny animals into open space, and they came back alive.
In September 2007 the TARDIS experiment on the ESA FOTON-M3 mission exposed dehydrated tardigrades to the vacuum, cold and radiation of low Earth orbit for ten days. Most survived the vacuum and cosmic rays, a few even survived unfiltered solar UV, and the survivors later laid eggs that hatched normally. The results were published in Current Biology in 2008.
What other animal could survive space?
